stories.headline: On Roberto Clemente Day, MLB has a Puerto Rico problem
stories.summary: The pipeline from the Hall of Famer's homeland to the major leagues is disintegrating.
stories.body:
KELVIN COLÓN WAS bouncing between ballparks in Puerto Rico last Tuesday, scouting teams in the inaugural Buzzer Beater baseball tournament, an unprecedented event featuring 32 high schools from across the island. Never had the baseball-loving nation held a full-fledged tournament featuring public schools, private schools and baseball academies.

Some teams were overmatched. The great majority of the players won't have professional baseball careers. But Colón, a scout for the Los Angeles Dodgers, was encouraged.

"There's talent here, man," Colón said. "I just left the ballpark right now, saw two guys that I could easily say are seventh-to-10th-round follows. They might end up in the 12th, 13th round, but that doesn't mean that they're not big leaguers."

Insiders from across Puerto Rico's baseball spectrum -- current and former major leaguers, front office executives, agents and scouts -- agree with Colón. Real talent exists in Puerto Rico -- and Tuesday's Roberto Clemente Day is a reminder of that. Major League Baseball's annual remembrance of the Hall of Fame outfielder, who died in a plane crash in 1972 delivering supplies to earthquake victims in Nicaragua, is a celebration of Clemente's marvelous career and humanitarian efforts. He's a hero across baseball-playing nations in Latin America, and nowhere more so than in his native Puerto Rico.

Clemente was the island's first baseball superstar, and his tragic death only added to his lore. He inspired generations of Puerto Ricans to pick up the sport and follow his path to the major leagues. But more than a half century after his death, nearly two dozen people interviewed for this story said that in recent years the pipeline from Puerto Rico to the majors has disintegrated.

The reasons they gave are wide-ranging, but every source pointed to one genesis for the decline: MLB's decision to include Puerto Rico, an unincorporated territory of the United States, in the Rule 4 draft in 1989. The move took Puerto Ricans out of the international market, where they could sign as free agents at 16 years old, and into a player pool with high school seniors from the United States.

"We are neither one thing nor the other," an agent based in Puerto Rico said. "We're not a state, we're not independent. In the draft we're Americans, but in the Futures Game we're part of the world. They decide where to put us.

"Being part of the draft, I can tell you, is definitely what has hurt us the most."

THE DECLINE OF Puerto Rican-born major leaguers was evident this July in Philadelphia. For the first time since 1988, no Puerto Rican-born players were on either All-Star team. In the days leading up to the Midsummer Classic, just five players born in Puerto Rico were selected in the 2026 MLB draft, none of them before the 13th round. No Puerto Rican-born player has been taken in the first round since Heliot Ramos in 2017.

So far this season, 27 players born in Puerto Rico have appeared in games. In 2001, that number was 54 -- exactly twice as many. New York Mets shortstop Francisco Lindor, who missed more than two months with a left calf strain, leads Puerto Rican-born players with 1.9 bWAR this season. That would've ranked 13th among Puerto Rican-born players in 2001. There are also no Puerto Rican-born players on Kiley McDaniel's top 100 prospects list.

The lack of depth became apparent during the World Baseball Classic in March, when several of Puerto Rico's best active MLB players, including veterans Lindor, Carlos Correa, Jose Berrios and Javier Baez, were unable to participate, largely due to injuries. Puerto Rico's tournament ended with a quarterfinal loss to Italy.

"It's poor right now," a longtime MLB front office executive said. "You can see that from the beginning with the World Baseball Classic this year."

The issues transcend baseball. A poverty rate more than double that of Mississippi -- the poorest state in the U.S. -- leaves families unable to keep up with the showcase culture that has engulfed youth baseball in the United States. There is a lack of accessible facilities to properly train players. There are fewer competitive games for top-end talent. Other sports and entertainment options drain talent from the potential player pool.

"We are in a truly horrible place," the Puerto Rican agent said. "Like never before."

"It's f---ed," a current major leaguer said.

Carlos Delgado, who hit 473 home runs -- the most ever by a Puerto Rican -- across 17 MLB seasons, began his professional career after signing with the Toronto Blue Jays for $90,000 in October 1988. He was the penultimate Puerto Rican to sign as an international free agent before the draft was implemented on the island.

"We're victims of the draft," Delgado said in Spanish. "The draft has always hurt us."

Delgado was part of Puerto Rico's 1990s golden era, a storied group that included Hall of Famers Roberto Alomar, Edgar Martínez and Ivan Rodríguez, plus a slew of All-Stars, including Sandy Alomar Jr., Juan González, Bernie Williams, Carlos Baerga, Benito Santiago and Ruben Sierra. All were signed as international free agents before Puerto Rico was included in the draft.

MLB's decision to incorporate Puerto Rico in the draft, according to multiple people interviewed, had unforeseen negative consequences on the flow of talent to the majors. Previously, most big league franchises employed full-time scouts on the island who would invest in the development of prospects, knowing that a strong relationship -- and the right amount of money -- could convince players to sign with their organizations. With the draft, however, teams lost that control; any one of the other 29 teams could simply pick a desired player in the draft before them.

"I think the draft had a deleterious effect on Puerto Rico in terms of the developmental players," said Lou Melendez, a former MLB executive for 33 years with extensive experience in Puerto Rico. "Because clubs, in my estimation, were disincentivized from investing the way they were many years ago."

While clubs have backed off investing in Puerto Rico over the past 37 years, MLB has tried to compensate with funding and programs.

The league helped establish the Puerto Rico Baseball Academy and High School and has donated millions of dollars to it since its inception in 2001. In 2017, MLB donated $1 million to Puerto Rico for Hurricane Maria relief. In 2022, the league and the MLBPA donated $2 million for the building of a stadium for The Carlos Beltran Baseball Academy.

The league has also established Reviving Baseball in Inner Cities (RBI) programs on the island, currently runs a development program in four regions from September through May with more than 200 players, and holds a showcase every winter for the top 100 draft-eligible players, according to an MLB spokesperson.

"Puerto Rico has a long history of producing extraordinary Major League players who have made great contributions to the game both on and off the field," MLB wrote in a statement to ESPN. "We continue to invest in several programs aimed towards developing the next generation of Puerto Rican players in the big leagues."

MLB has played 49 regular-season games in Puerto Rico since 2001 and has had Puerto Rico host games in four of the six WBC tournaments, including this year's edition.

"The clubs don't invest, but the commissioner's office has," said Melendez, who served as Puerto Rico's general manager for the first three iterations of the WBC. "And it just hasn't been enough. It just hasn't been enough."

OVER THE YEARS, the Dominican Republic and Venezuela -- Latin American nations in the free agent market -- have seen major league clubs increase their investments, with more scouts and the creation of academies to help develop prospects. Theirs is far from a perfect situation; the system in the Dominican Republic is rife with corruption and exploitation. Still, 93 players from the Dominican Republic, including some of the sport's brightest stars, were on Opening Day rosters this season. Venezuela, whose pipeline has been damaged recently by political and economic instability, had 60 players on Opening Day rosters, second among countries and territories outside of the United States.

Puerto Rico, meanwhile, was left with a void in the developmental chain. Over the years, many teenage prospects have left Puerto Rico to attend high school in the U.S. That list includes Lindor, Báez and Edwin Arroyo, an infielder who was selected in the second round in 2021 and made his major league debut this season.

That's because unlike the U.S., Puerto Rico does not have an expansive high school baseball circuit. Baseball academies have been created over the past two decades in an attempt to fill the gap. The first one -- the Puerto Rico Baseball Academy and High School -- has produced multiple major leaguers, including Correa, a three-time All-Star and the only Puerto Rican ever drafted No. 1 overall. Carlos Beltrán, who became the sixth Puerto Rican inducted into the Hall of Fame in July and the first one who was drafted, opened his academy in 2011.

But the developmental gap, according to multiple sources, remains an issue. For one, neither academy offers dorm rooms for students, making accessibility an issue for many prospects. Sources also pointed to the lack of infrastructure available for high schoolers to train as a huge impediment, leaving the typical Puerto Rican draft prospect physically underdeveloped compared with his American and Latin American counterparts.

"I've always been a huge proponent of high school baseball in Puerto Rico," said Houston Astros manager Joe Espada, the only Puerto Rican manager in the majors and a second-round pick in 1996. "There are enough ballparks. And it doesn't have to be a league with 30 games. You can start with 10, 15."

The developmental deficiency continues after the draft, according to sources, making Puerto Rican prospects' rise through the minor leagues more difficult.

"You have the 18-year-old kid that signs out of an academy in Puerto Rico," a former major leaguer from Puerto Rico said. "He goes and plays ball. Where does he train during the offseason the next year? Or the year after? Or the year after? That 18-year-old kid isn't going to play in winter ball. He's not developed yet enough to play in winter ball where you have to win.

"So, where does he go? It's not like the 18-year-old kid in the United States that goes back to his unbelievable high school facility. Or goes to one of those institutions and can pay for it because there's an infrastructure in the U.S. In Puerto Rico, where do you go? A lot of them get stuck."

The quandary also extends to the classroom, according to sources. Ramos was Puerto Rico's top 2017 draft prospect when he decided to transfer from a public high school to Leadership Christian Academy, a bilingual private high school, for his senior year. The change required him to leave his family and move in with his current agent.

The San Francisco Giants drafted him 19th, and they agreed on a $3.1 million signing bonus. Looking back, the outfielder saw the move as pivotal in his preparation for draft negotiations, as he also had a commitment to Florida International University in his back pocket. On an island where most public schools lack sufficient English education, many of his peers don't have that advantage.

"There's a lot of people who don't know English in Puerto Rico," said Ramos, who was acquired by the New York Yankees last month. "So to go to the United States for college in a language you don't understand, that is intimidating."

That often hurts players' leverage when negotiating with teams, sources said, to the point that clubs believe they can select Puerto Ricans later in the draft and offer them less money than Americans knowing that their backup plans aren't as appealing.

"I've heard the comment from people that this is the island of $100K," Colón said. "Like everyone will sign for $100K or less."

Since 2018, three players from Puerto Rico have been selected in the second round and two have been taken in the third round. This year, Juriel Collazo was the island's first draft pick. He was chosen in the 13th round with the 374th selection.

SEVERAL PEOPLE INTERVIEWED for this story emphasized their belief that Puerto Rico would suffer another significant setback if MLB's recent draft proposal to the Major League Baseball Players Association were to pass. The proposal, extended in June during the parties' ongoing CBA negotiations, calls for the domestic draft to shrink from 20 rounds to 12 rounds and for players to be at least two years removed from high school graduation, rendering high school seniors ineligible.

"We never made the adjustment fully to what the draft was and what it became," the former Puerto Rican big leaguer said. "And we're looking at like 30 years ago. Culturally, we were one way for a long time. And this is the outcome. Now we're at 20 rounds and it's even more difficult."

Sources said they believe Puerto Rico would be better off returning to the international free agent market or being included in an international draft if that is introduced as part of the next collective bargaining agreement. Melendez said he supports removing Puerto Rico from the draft for five to 10 years.

"Let's run an experiment," Melendez said. "You can count the draft picks on two hands every year, so why not take them out of the draft and let's see what happens. Let's try something because what we're doing now ain't working. It's not working."

But a few warned that the change wouldn't singlehandedly repair the pipeline, which would require time and significant investment.

"We'd be competing against a huge group of people that are more developed at ages 15, 16, 17," a longtime scout in Puerto Rico said. "It would take years to figure out."

Others worry about the potential damage a change could inflict beyond baseball.

"I don't want free agency for Puerto Rico, and that has nothing to do with the game. It has to do with the social aspect," a Puerto Rican former All-Star said. "In the Dominican Republic, they're signing kids at 16 years old, but a lot of those kids leave school at 12, 13 years old to go practice every day to see if they have a chance to sign professionally.

"And what happens? The majority of the players aren't going to play in the major leagues, so what you're doing is putting a bunch of 17-, 18-year-old kids in Dominican society without a high school degree. I think if free agency were to come to Puerto Rico, maybe it wouldn't happen at first, but I think in the long term what happens in the Dominican could happen here."

Colón is now one of a dying breed: a full-time scout for an MLB club who is based in Puerto Rico. He has been with the Dodgers since 2018 after stints with the Miami Marlins and Baltimore Orioles and now splits his time between the island and South Florida -- two areas he is responsible for covering for the two-time defending World Series champions. Colón, who is also the general manager of the Caguas Criollos in the Puerto Rican winter league, said he knows of just two other full-time MLB scouts who live in Puerto Rico.

"If you're living on the island, you're doing something else to solidify that full-time role," Colón said. "I just think what's hurt Puerto Rico, it goes all the way back to the draft."

But Colón is not as pessimistic as some of his peers. He pointed to the six players from Puerto Rico, an island with a population of 3.2 million people, who made their major league debuts this season as an encouraging sign. He argued that U.S. states with similar populations don't produce those numbers, and yet "people are banging on Puerto Rico."

Some data supports his sentiment. Puerto Rico produced 25 high school draft selections in the top 20 rounds from 2021 through 2025, ranking in the top 10 each year when compared with U.S. states. Per capita, Puerto Rico produced twice as many players on Opening Day rosters this season as Venezuela, which has a population of 28.6 million, though the country's recent turmoil has significantly impacted clubs' ability to invest in and unearth talent there.

Colón sees stronger future draft classes in his scouting trips around Puerto Rico. Maybe Puerto Rico will never relive its 1990s golden era or generate a wave of All-Star talent like the one headed by Lindor, Correa and Báez in the 2010s. But he's hopeful -- to an extent.

"The forecast of the future, yeah, it's cloudy," Colón said. "I admit that part -- it's cloudy."

stories.headline: NHL superstar poll: Rule changes, Texas expansion, fan culture
stories.summary: We asked a panel of stars at the NHL/NHLPA player media tour for their takes on a variety of hot topics.
stories.body:
HENDERSON, Nev. -- With training camps opening up this week, I caught up with over two dozen NHL superstars to get their takes on vital and trivial issues.

Some of hockey's biggest names discuss NHL rule changes they'd like to see; how an 84-game regular season will impact them; how they feel about the current state of fan culture; as well as their offseason life highlights and what they'd name a new expansion team in Houston or Austin, Texas.

Interviews were conducted at the NHL/NHLPA player media tour last week in Las Vegas. Enjoy!

How to watch the 2026-27 NHL season on ESPN networks, including 100 exclusive games and the out-of-market package (over 1,050 games).

What was your favorite experience of the summer?
"My dad finding out he got into the Hall of Fame. He honestly played it off so cool. But that first moment of him telling us, you could see the smile on his face. That was pretty special." -- Brady Tkachuk, Florida Panthers

"Lots of concerts. I went to Luke Combs, which was actually an awesome concert. Got to meet him afterward, and he was just an amazing guy. I mean, he's a Hurricanes fan, so I wasn't happy about that, but he was an amazing guy." -- Matthew Schaefer, New York Islanders

"We did a family trip to Cabo. It's nice to get away from real life for a minute and just shut everything down and just be present with your family. My wife and three kids, and then my parents and my aunt and uncle. The more, the merrier." -- Tage Thompson, Buffalo Sabres

"Going to the World Cup final. Got to go with a bunch of buddies, so it made it fun." -- Trevor Zegras, Philadelphia Flyers

"I just went to Spain with my family. Mallorca. Just chilled there and didn't do much." -- Leo Carlsson, Anaheim Ducks

"Our family did a little get-together in Michigan, just on the lake, on the water. We all took five days off and just spent time together, fished, hung out, played games. Caught a couple bass, pike. It was really good fishing waters. I had my girlfriend out, and she was out-fishing me, catching these huge bass. It was pretty sad." -- Frank Nazar, Chicago Blackhawks

"My favorite experience was flying back home to Stockholm for a week and bringing my two older kids. They're now 6 and 5 years old and they really hadn't experienced Sweden because they were 1 and 2 last time they went. It was just so awesome getting to see my hometown through their eyes for the first time. Showing them where I grew up and seeing all of our Swedish friends and family. So it was really great. That was my absolute favorite week of the summer." -- Gabriel Landeskog, Colorado Avalanche

"I got married in Vancouver just with our families, and then we had a big celebration in Minnesota. I actually was a little nervous. I didn't think I was going to get nervous, but yeah, I was a little nervous for the whole wedding part." -- Brock Boeser, Vancouver Canucks

"My day with the Cup. It was a good day with friends, family, and then got to eat some really good food out of it. Some barbecue and a Slavin Sundae: ice cream, brownies, Heath bits, chocolate fudge, red sprinkles." -- Jaccob Slavin, Carolina Hurricanes

"I went to Scotland on a golf trip. That was probably my favorite. A couple good rounds, actually. Overall, it was just cool to experience those courses." -- Alex DeBrincat, Detroit Red Wings

"I was able to buy a cottage up in Muskoka [Ontario], so just being able to share that with my family. I had some friends up there. It was pretty cool." -- Quinton Byfield, Los Angeles Kings

"My newborn. That's the best experience I could have asked for." -- Zach Werenski, Columbus Blue Jackets

"I had a kid. It's been awesome." -- Jack Eichel, Vegas Golden Knights

The NHL is adding another team in Texas, in either Houston or Austin. What would you like for them to be called?
"The Houston Humidity." -- Wyatt Johnston, Dallas Stars

"I guess it depends what city. But maybe the Rattlers or something?" -- Thompson

"It's got to be something bull-riding related maybe. Rodeo-related. Bull Riders. There you go." -- Jack Hughes, New Jersey Devils

"The Houston Hammers." -- Jamie Drysdale, Flyers

"The Austin Cattle." -- Eichel

"The Ranchers." -- Boeser

"The Mustangs." -- Macklin Celebrini, San Jose Sharks

"The Houston Aeros. Run it back." -- Cole Caufield, Montreal Canadiens

"The Butt-Kickers. Because of the boots." -- Filip Forsberg, Nashville Predators

"I was going to say Cowboys. I think it's baller. Would make a sick logo, too." -- Logan Cooley, Utah Mammoth

"Maybe the Houston Sparks? Spurs, Sparks? I don't know." -- Slavin

"The Wranglers. Oh no, that's Calgary. Eh, we can do the same name for Texas." -- Tkachuk

"Every time I think of Texas, I just keep thinking of other teams' names. I mean, I like the Longhorns." -- Byfield

"Texas Hockey Club." -- Zegras

"Not for me to decide." -- Tom Wilson, Washington Capitals

How will your life be impacted by an 84-game season?
"My life will not be impacted by it." -- Matt Coronato, Calgary Flames

"I don't think it will be. Now, we play four preseason games, and I can only play two. And previously we had seven, so at the end of the day, I think you're still really playing the same amount of games." -- Thompson

"Impacted for the better. Shorter training camp, less preseason games. I feel like it just kind of becomes a drag a little bit when you're playing four preseason games." -- Werenski

"Just more time on the ice. Nothing better than that." -- Tkachuk

"I feel like the beginning of the season is going to be a little more offensively open. Obviously, having a bunch of preseason games and longer training camp gets you into your structure a little bit more and a little more comfortable. So, I feel like the start might be a little more chaotic, but it's just two more games, and I'm excited to play more hockey." -- Byfield

"I think the fact that they started the season early to spread out the games, I think we won't notice it as much." -- Jake Guentzel, Tampa Bay Lightning

"I think once you get past the 50-game mark, it kind of blends, to be honest with you. So, I think the extra two and probably the two preseason games that you miss out on will kind of even out." -- Drysdale

"Shorter preseason is going to be huge. But more back-to-back [games], which is going to be a shame." -- Zegras

"I don't think it really changes much. I think once you're in the grind and you just keep focused on that and a couple extra games won't be a big deal." -- Wilson

"I don't think it'll be too bad. Two extra games. Eighty-two is a lot of games; 84, you're not feeling any necessarily different, I think. I think we'll all be alright." -- Matty Beniers, Seattle Kraken

"I think your total workload for the year with the shortened preseason is pretty similar. Maybe you get a chance to get a couple more points." -- Robert Thomas, St. Louis Blues

"I'm excited. Two more games is always fun when you can play more hockey." -- Schaefer

"More chances to shoot the puck." -- Caufield

If you could change or drop one rule in the NHL, what would it be?
"Not so much of a rule as it's a judgment call, but it's when you call a tripping and an embellishment at the same time. Oh my God, it drives me nuts. And I'm always talking to the refs about it, and they're like, 'Well, I don't know.' It's really like it just has to be one or the other. I think that's common sense. I understand there can be a little bit of both, but if you're giving out a penalty, just pick one. Which one was worse? Was the dive worse or was the tripping worse?" -- Landeskog

"If you score on a power play, they don't come out of the box. You just keep your power play. Full two minutes, no matter what." -- Coronato

"Icing the puck on the penalty kill. Hate it." -- Zegras

"I just think if you score a short-hand goal, the guy's penalty should be done." -- Guentzel

"Delay of game. Puck over the glass. I don't think there's a person in the history of the game who purposefully puts the puck over the glass." -- Drysdale

"The puck-over-the-glass penalty. I've had too many of those. I won the Lady Byng [in 2020-21], and my one penalty was puck over the glass. That's not why I'm against it, but that's just a good example of it being a silly penalty." -- Slavin

"The league's always looking for more goals. Fans want more goals. If you took away goals being taken down because of a kicking motion, I think that's something that would instantly change it. You'd have a lot more goals. I think, also, if you're skilled enough to be able to use your feet to redirect the puck or kick it when you're tied up in front of the net, I think that should be a goal. I mean, obviously, you don't want guys just kicking at it all the time. I get the injury-prevention stuff there. But, at the same time, it's not as much of a true kicking where your blade's coming up. If you've worked hard enough and you put the puck in the net, it should be a goal." -- Thompson

"Getting kicked out of the faceoff. I might be be the guy who got kicked out the most." -- Byfield

"How the rookies have to wear helmets during warmups. I'd love to take a bucket off. I think that'd be nice." -- Schaefer

"No offsides. Get a few more breakaways." -- Cooley

"Just take off offsides completely. Play it like it's roller hockey where you could just be anywhere on the ice. The whole game would change. Like, do you take the power play and let the guy just cherry pick all the way down? But then he might have a breakaway. And I think the whole game would be different." -- Nazar

"The rule where when we dump it in on the goalie, sometimes we're not allowed to change. I don't know what the point of that rule." -- Boeser

"I honestly would let people travel day of games if they want to. Sometimes, we do it for Christmas games, usually where we go to St. Louis. But instead of flying the day before, for us, to Carolina or Detroit, some of those cities where you can just morning skate at home and go right to the game type of thing." -- Forsberg

"I like goalies playing the puck, so I would take out the dead space in the corners. The trapezoid. Especially with our goalies." -- Thomas

"Goals on high sticks, like tip-ins. I say if it looks like a skill, I think it should be counted." -- Caufield

"Add more time to 3-on-3 overtime. I don't love the shootout. I would rather someone wins in overtime. So, instead of five [minutes], maybe 15 or 10 or even 20. I don't know." -- Beniers

"I think the league's really good now. Anything that continues to keep guys healthy and safe and limit big injuries, I'm a proponent of, but I think the league's in a good spot." -- Quinn Hughes, Minnesota Wild

"The one thing is the offsides [review]. It's so hard, but at some point, it's like if you're a centimeter off 30 seconds before the goal, I think just leave it as a good goal. I think it's better for the game. I think that's where it gets hard though, because it's like in a playoff game you might be upset that it was offside, but I don't know what the right way to do it is. You think with AI now, you could almost just have it automatic, like they have in soccer for the offside." -- Johnston

"The offside review, when it's long after the play. If it's offside and they score right away, it should be offside. But if it's 30 seconds after and then the team scores, it's like, 'Oh, come on.' It doesn't affect the play. But I do love it when the other team scores, and then it's offside." -- Carlsson

"I think we're getting pretty nitpicky on all these different rules, like leg up over the blue line, all the cameras. Too much gets screwed up. As we get crazier and crazier, it's just counterproductive. I just want to go back and play it like it was in the 1800s or whenever the game was invented." -- Wilson

How do you feel about hockey fan culture in 2026, like how they engage with you in person and on social media?
"They're passionate, that's for sure. So, you've got to love the passion." -- Tkachuk

"I think it's great, with the way the game's trending and the amount of attention it's getting. Social media obviously has kind of been pushing that. Fans being able to interact with players a little bit more than they've been used to is something that they like. I know from a few of my buddies, they love following along with a lot of the behind-the-scenes stuff and things that fans usually don't get to see -- the curtain being pulled back for some of these fans that have been watching hockey for a long time." -- Thompson

"I love our fans in the league. They make it special. The playoffs in Minnesota are amazing. Dallas was great. Colorado was great. I try not to focus too much on engagement and social media and whatnot, just because there's a lot of negativity out there. But when you run into a fan in person and they're just a true fan of the game; that's always nice to see." -- Quinn Hughes

"I think obviously everything online is crazy, but I think 2026 was a great year for hockey and its fans, just with Olympics and the brand and the young talent coming up. I think there's a lot of players that people can root for." -- Jack Hughes

"I love it. There are definitely a lot more rivalries online. You can feel it in arenas and it's fun. I think we're starting to get more and more European soccer atmospheres at games, and it's starting to grow in that area. I think the more involved fans are in the game, the more you feel them on the ice; it's just awesome." -- Thomas

"I love it. When I'm in Chicago, I get a lot of great, positive things. I'm walking down the street, someone will be like, 'Hey man, let's go this year. Good luck.' I love that stuff. I think it's great. The fans are what make the sport, right? Yeah. I mean, we're here to play hockey and entertain, but they're what keeps the stadium full and what keeps us wanting to go back at it day in, day out." -- Nazar

"I think there's a great momentum behind the game right now. Obviously, everybody has an avenue to say whatever they want at any time, so that's always interesting. But it's part of the gig." -- Wilson

"I think it's cool to interact with fans. You always want to give a great impression. Ever since we moved [to Utah], they've been super supportive of us and have given us everything. They've been unbelievable people. So, I think anytime you could be nice to people and make someone's day, it means a lot to them." -- Cooley

"I'd say they're a bit ruthless at times. But for the most part, they're great people. There's just a lot of negativity and that stuff always sticks a little bit more, which is unfortunate. But not all people are like that. We've got great fans in Philadelphia, very supportive, so they're great." -- Zegras

"I think with the betting now in sports, they're a little more intense online. But we're lucky in Tampa. They're a great fan base. They support us well, and we're obviously lucky to have them." -- Guentzel

"I think the more access that you have, I think it brings people more into the sport. I think the more you meet the people behind the players, the more obviously you'll enjoy the game personally. There's a lot of good guys. The more you can personalize people, the better it'll be." -- Drysdale

"I'd say I have mixed feelings about it. I think there's parts of it that are great, but then there are parts of it are not great." -- Slavin

"I mean obviously, a lot of fans are great. Most of the fans are really great. They're great in public, too, when I see them. It's always going to be some guys on the Internet who are going to talk s---, of course. [With the offer sheet], obviously some guys could tell you to do whatever and some guys said, 'I'm so happy for you,' and all that stuff. So it's something that I'm used to, too. I'm not really getting offended by that." -- Carlsson

"I think everyone has an opinion. I think in person, players are more accessible now than ever. Not a bad thing. Fans are what make the sport good and grow the game. So obviously, you want as many fans to be having great experiences as you can. In saying that, sometimes it could be a little much, I guess, especially with what I went through [this offseason]. But it's all a part of it." -- Werenski

"I feel like hockey fans are the best fans. They're so passionate. You're getting booed, you're getting chirped. I love how everybody has their opinions. And the thing is, I don't care what their opinions are, to be honest. I just want to worry about myself and the Islanders' fans because they're the best fans in the league, and they're the ones I'm worried about." -- Schaefer

"My favorite, especially in Denver and Colorado, is meeting people out. Our fans are so great. They never want to bother you. They never want to hassle you. All they want to do is say 'hi,' shake your hand, maybe take a picture and that's it. It's not, 'Why did you do this? Why'd you do that? Why did you guys lose that?' It's just like, 'Hey man, go get them. Good luck. Best of luck.' They're so gracious that way. They care, they're supportive, but also they understand that we're humans. They see us out and about quite a bit. Families eating dinner, doing whatever we're doing, and they see that there's a human element to what we do." -- Landeskog

stories.headline: No stadium, no problems as Devils look to build roster
stories.summary: The Tasmania Devils chief executive has played down concerns that a contentious stadium will impact the club's ability to attract star AFL talent.
stories.body:
The Tasmania Devils believe an unfinished stadium won't hurt their prospects of luring players to the club as they prepare to announce their first batch of signings.

Speaking at Canberra's Parliament House on Tuesday, the club's chief executive Brendon Gale played down concerns surrounding the contentious Macquarie Point Stadium in Hobart.

The $1.13 billion venue won't be ready in time when the Devils' AFL and AFLW teams enter the league in 2028, and will be primed for the 2031 season.

Tasmania plans to split its home games between Hobart's Bellerive Oval and Launceston's UTAS Stadium in the first years of its AFL campaign instead.

The stadium concerns come as the club looks to land the signatures of marquee names when they are allowed to lure 18 uncontracted players from rival clubs across 2027-28.

But in a possible precursor to the challenges that lie ahead, young gun Logan Morris re-signed with Brisbane despite the Devils taking an interest in him.

Even without a state-of-the-art stadium and no Morris, Gale remains confident in their ability to recruit players to the Apple Isle.

"We have an incredible high-performance centre which is being built, and that'll be 9,000 square metres and an elite environment to come and work and realise your potential as a male or female athlete," Gale said.

"I think those things are probably more important, and I don't expect (no stadium) to have an impact on getting players at all.

"When the stadium comes along in 2031, there'll be another big sugar hit. There'll be so much anticipation, excitement again."

In the NRL, the Perth Bears have struggled to pin down a marquee player ahead of their entrance into the competition next season, while fellow expansion club PNG Chiefs have inked deals with several star names because of lucrative tax-free contracts.

Regardless, media reports have emerged the Devils will unveil their first batch of players later this month, which will be under-17 prospects, after the league allowed the team to sign a maximum of 12 under-17 athletes across 2026 and 2027.

The club's entrance is set to create another conundrum for the AFL, as it considers whether it should shorten games, as it may need to expand the number of rounds to cater for the new team.

Jack Riewoldt, a former Richmond premiership winner and Tasmanian local, said the changes were above his pay grade.

"The game continues to evolve. The rules continue to evolve to make sure not only is it safe for the players, but user experience and viewership can be at their most prevalent," he said.

stories.headline: Allianz Arena to host 2028 Champions League final, Camp Nou to host in 2029
stories.summary: The Munich Football Arena and Barcelona's Spotify Camp Nou will host the 2028 and 2029 UEFA Champions League finals, European football's governing body confirmed Tuesday.
stories.body:
The Munich Football Arena and Barcelona's Spotify Camp Nou will host the 2028 and 2029 UEFA Champions League finals, European football's governing body confirmed Tuesday.

Bayern Munich's stadium -- also known as the Allianz Arena for sponsorship reasons -- held the 2025 and 2012 finals, but it will be the first time in exactly 30 years that Camp Nou has been the venue for the biggest game in European club football.

Camp Nou last hosted the final in 1999, when Manchester United famously scored two late goals to beat Bayern 2-1 to claim the second of their three European Cups.

While the 70,000-capacity Allianz Arena is ready to go, Camp Nou is still being redeveloped as part of a revamp which began in 2023.

After over two years playing away from their home stadium, Barça returned to Camp Nou last November, but work is still ongoing.

The capacity is currently capped at 62,000, with the third tier yet to be completed and the roof still to be put on.

Barça estimate that the stadium, which will eventually hold 105,000 fans, will be finished towards the end of 2027 -- or at the latest by 2028.

- 2026 Ballon d'Or: Full men's, women's short lists, host city change, more

- Ousmane Dembélé: 'Never the chosen one,' but hard work at 'back of the class' earned Ballon d'Or

This season's Champions League final will be played at Atlético Madrid's Metropolitano Stadium.

There was also confirmation Tuesday that the Parc Olympic Lyonnais and the National Stadium of Wales in Cardiff will host the 2028 and 2029 UEFA Women's Champions League finals, respectively.

Meanwhile, the 2028 and 2029 UEFA Europa League finals will be played at the National Arena in Bucharest and the National Stadium Serbia in Belgrade.

The UEFA Conference League showpieces in the same years will take place at Juventus Stadium in Turin and the Puskás Aréna in Budapest.

Finally, the 2027 UEFA Super Cup with be played at the Johan Cruyff Arena in Amsterdam and the 2028 edition will be hosted by the Astana Arena in Astana.

stories.headline: Max vs 100: How Verstappen's karting years made an F1 champion - and prepared him for an all-new test
stories.summary: Max Verstappen tells ESPN's Laurence Edmondson how his karting roots shaped his F1 career and prepared him for the Max vs 100 challenge.
stories.body:
On Sept. 16, Max Verstappen will attempt to overtake 100 other drivers in a unique go-karting challenge at Silverstone, live on Disney+. Ahead of the event, ESPN caught up with the four-time world champion to discuss his long history of go-karting and the years he spent honing his skills at tracks across Europe.

Between the ages of four and 15, Max Verstappen's life revolved around go-kart tracks.

Weekends would be spent racing all around Europe, initially close to home in Belgium and the Netherlands and then further afield in Italy, Spain and the U.K. in his early teens.

His father, Jos, a former Formula 1 driver, would load Max's kart into the back of their van ahead of every race weekend and drive his son across the length and breadth of Europe to the next event. During the height of Max's karting career, Jos calculated they were clocking up more than 60,000 motorway miles per year as the father-and-son team hoovered up trophies on a path destined for F1.

"It was a really nice period in my life," Max recalls. "All different kinds of conditions, tracks, travels.

- Max vs 100: Meet the drivers racing against Red Bull's Verstappen

- Max vs 100: F1 drivers predict how Verstappen will fare racing 100 drivers

- What makes Max Verstappen so good? Career, background and F1 records

"Sometimes it wasn't even the race weekend I loved the most, but just the travel experience together with my dad; in the van, talking a lot about life, talking a lot about the current, but also, of course, where we were trying to head to.

"For sure, go-karting has been a massive part of my life."

On weekdays, Jos would pick Max up after school and take him directly to his workshop to work on his kart engines. Max was encouraged to get his hands dirty from an early age, and the hours of tinkering after school would only come to an end when it was time to head home for dinner. Once they'd eaten, Max would go up to bed and Jos would return to the workshop, sometimes until midnight, until every last performance advantage had been found.

"My dad was my mechanic and my engine tuner as well," Max recalls. "We had our own dyno also in the workshop, so we did a lot in-house.

"I know a lot of dads are mechanics or they work with their son, but I don't know anyone that has done it so intensively.

"My dad really understood what was needed from the go-kart, but also from the engine."

The local kart circuit in Genk, Belgium became the Verstappens' second home. All through the year Max would take to the track multiple times a week to test new parts while learning to brake later, rotate the kart more precisely, and get on the throttle earlier.

Even in the wet winter months when other karters would pack up early and go home, the Verstappens would continue to clock up the mileage. Max would stay out on track until his hands felt frozen to the bone and he could barely feel his fingertips.

"I would warm my gloves on the exhaust because it's quite hot," he says with a smile. "You could put your gloves on it for a little bit and then take them off and they would be warm.

"It works really well, but the problem is when you're really cold and you heat them up your fingers swell up because of the increase of blood flow. Sometimes you were driving a bit with thick hands. But it all makes you tougher as a driver and as a kid at the time."

'You only get one shot at this'

The school Max was attending in Belgium didn't recognise go-karting as a sport, which made it difficult to get exemptions from class for races on the other side of Europe. When he did, the young Verstappen tried to focus on his homework during those 10- or 12-hour road trips in the van, but ultimately his schoolwork never came as easily as the karting trophies.

"It was tough. Sometimes I would come back home and you arrive on a Monday back, and you've kind of missed a week of lecturing and you try to catch up within two or three days of what was missed.

"With that already I didn't like school, so it was a bit tough.

"I always targeted to do something in life where school was not necessary. Plus, at the same time, I always said to myself, even if it doesn't work out in racing I can always go back to school.

"You only get one shot at this. If you fail because you try to catch up on school, I think I would always kick myself. School you can always catch up on."

It's hard to believe now, but early in Max's karting journey there was a moment when Jos wasn't sure if his son had the talent to make it all the way to F1. He had been karting for over a year and making steady progress, but then, ahead of his sixth birthday, the lap times stopped improving.

"I think there was a time when my dad was questioning it a little bit," Max says. "We always went to that same track in Genk, and at one point I stalled a little bit -- when you are four years old naturally there is a progression, but I think around five-and-a-half or six years old it was like I plateaued. We went again and again and again and I didn't really get faster.

"I just kept being a couple of tenths off what I needed to be, of the older guys because that is what you compare yourself to. Then my dad had a good idea. We went to a different track for the first time, so I drove somewhere new for the first time.

"It actually went really well on that particular track, so when I went back to Genk it also clicked and I suddenly just picked up pace.

"Maybe my mind needed a little reset of just seeing different corners and a different combination of corners.

"I spoke about it with my dad years later, but I remember the scene of going to Genk over and over again and going to that other track for the first time, I do remember that.

"At the time I didn't know that my dad was so worried about my pace, but I do remember the sequence because it went really well on that particular track. My dad was like, 'tomorrow we go again but to Genk.' I was like 'alright, sure. I drive wherever.'"

- Max vs 100 explained: Rules, drivers, shortcuts and how Verstappen can win

Was there ever a time when Max didn't enjoy the endless pursuit of lap time?

"I always loved it and I think you always want to go out and go fast," he says.

"But of course there are also moments where maybe it's not going so well. You don't love it to 100%. But at the end of the day I would always wake up the next day wanting to go.

"It's like in life. There are better days and there are worse days."

How Jos Verstappen prepared Max for F1

In Jos, Max had a mechanic, an engineer and a driver coach. Every time they arrived for a test session, there would be a plan to ensure every lap resulted in progress towards the end goal of winning the next race, fighting for the next championship, and inching closer to the dream of F1.

"When we went karting there was always a clear strategy behind it with my dad, in terms of what we were practicing," Max says.

"My dad never said to me 'just go out and have fun.' No, we go out because we're testing or preparing. There was always a very strict strategy behind it.

"Even when we would go on summer holidays, of course we would also spend time on the beach, but we had go-karting days where we would create mini races.

"So one time I would start first, then second, third, last. With however many people we were with, which was mainly 7-8 people maximum. So one time you start first, then last, or you're in the middle.

"We would create these little start scenarios and overtaking scenarios. It was really fun."

The nostalgia Max feels for those endless days of karting is almost tangible as he sits in Red Bull's F1 paddock hospitality. The dream he had as a kid was ultimately fulfilled in 2021 when he won his first Formula 1 title before going on to take three more over the following three years.

Now a father himself, it begs the question of whether he can see himself becoming a karting dad?

"You don't know," he says. "I think what is always very important as a parent is that you support them in whatever they want to do.

"It doesn't matter if you're a boy or a girl, but for me, I'm not going to be the parent that is going to push them into a racing scenario. If they want to do it, sure. I will make sure that she or he will have the best possibilities.

"But I'm not going to actively push it. They need to want it.

"I hope they do something else -- I hope they play tennis or play football!"

Max vs 100: Can Verstappen pass them all?

The freezing cold test days and overtaking drills during his summer holidays will likely come in useful next week as Max attempts to pass 100 karts on a specially designed kart track at Silverstone. The furthest back he can remember starting on a grid during his karting career was 10th or 11th and he hasn't driven a competitive go-kart since 2016 (his track days away from F1 are now firmly focused on GT racing).

"A hundred is a lot, you know, but I think how they've set up the track from what they've shown me, I think it will be good," Max says of the challenge. "But it's still going to be hectic, for sure."

And in terms of a strategy, will Max, to borrow one of his own phrases, go "full send"?

"I think I first need to understand and see the level between drivers.

"I also don't like to overthink the situation. I just need to go with the flow and try to make the best of it.

"I'm hoping that with my background, I should be faster than most. I hope! I mean, it would be quite embarrassing if they're faster than me!"

Max vs 100: When and how do I watch it?
Max vs 100 is taking place on Sept. 16, and will be shown live in the UK on Disney+.

In the U.S., Max vs 100 will also air on the ESPN App for Unlimited subscribers before a delayed ESPN2 broadcast later that day.

The race itself will start at 6 p.m., with the live stream beginning one hour before.

Comedian Mo Gilligan will front the coverage, which is set to include drone footage and live race data.

stories.headline: Source: Colombia, U.S. battling for Inter Miami U20 dual national Alexander Shaw
stories.summary: Inter Miami midfielder Alexander Shaw has been contacted by Colombia after playing for the United States U-20 team in the 2026 Concacaf tournament, a source confirmed to ESPN.
stories.body:
Inter Miami midfielder Alexander Shaw is currently being pursued by both Colombia and the United States on a youth Under 20 level, a source confirmed to ESPN.

He previously featured for the United States youth national team in the 2026 Concacaf U20 champion, reaching the final after a perfect group stage. Shaw helped the USYNT to victories against Haiti, El Salvador and Cuba without conceding a goal.

Shaw scored in the 5-0 victory over Cuba.

The USYNT concluded the tournament as runners-up after falling 2-0 to Mexico.

Shaw has previously received call ups from the Colombia U20, but a source confirms that all requests have been declined by Inter Miami for occurring during Major League Soccer regular season action.

Shaw, however, joined the Colombian national team during the World Cup as a sparring under manager Nestor Lorenzo while the squad trained in Miami.

A source confirmed to ESPN that both Colombia and the United States are looking for Shaw to join the team for the upcoming U-20 World Cup in 2027.

Inter Miami recently signed Shaw to a contract through the end of the 2026 MLS season, with options to extend through June 2027, the 2027-28 and 2028-29 seasons.

He's made five appearances this season and recorded a goal in the 7-1 victory over CF Montreal.

stories.headline: Tom Aspinall vacates UFC heavyweight title amid ongoing eye issues
stories.summary: Tom Aspinall has decided to vacate his UFC heavyweight title as a result of "ongoing complications" with injuries to his eyes.
stories.body:
Tom Aspinall has decided to vacate his UFC heavyweight title as a result of "ongoing complications" with injuries to his eyes.

The Brit confirmed his decision via a statement on social media on Monday, saying he was "gutted." Aspinall (15-3) said he had been back sparring and had a new fight date locked in, but an accident in training has brought a further set-back.

Aspinall has not fought since his no contest against Ciryl Gane last October, when he was poked in the eyes. He was forced to retire from the fight in the first round and has since had multiple surgeries in both his eyes.

"Ongoing complications with my eyes mean I cannot get medically cleared to fight right now," Aspinall said.

"I've had multiple surgeries, accidents and infections, and done everything possible to get back to competing.

"I had previously agreed to a fight date and was back sparring, feeling great and ready to compete when an accident caused further damage to my right eye. This means more time away from the sport, and right now, the timing of my return is unclear.

"I've now made the decision to vacate the heavyweight title. I've asked the UFC to allow me to make this statement because I don't want to hold the heavyweight division up. I know what it's like to have your career put on hold and I want the other fighters to have the opportunity to compete for the title."

In June, Aspinall confirmed he was back in full training and working towards a rematch with Gane, who beat Alex Pereira that month.

Following Gane's win over Pereira, Aspinall said on his YouTube channel that the was ready for a rematch with the Frenchman and prepared to fight in Paris.

Aspinall stressed he wanted to return to action as soon as possible but on the advice of doctors, would not be fighting in the foreseeable future.

"We have worked closely with different doctors and specialists to try and make my return happen, but unfortunately, it's simply not possible right now," he said. "I'm absolutely gutted. I've chased this dream since I was 10 years old.

"I'm not done. Stepping away from the title is not stepping away from the sport or the dream. I'll continue doing everything I can to get healthy, get cleared and get back to competing as soon as possible."

stories.headline: Roosters make Walker call as half's absence laid bare
stories.summary: James Tedesco says Daly Cherry-Evans took ownership of his off night against Penrith, as the Sydney Roosters aim to knock Cronulla out of the finals.
stories.body:
James Tedesco claims it would be unfair to lay the blame for the Sydney Roosters' last-gasp finals loss to Penrith at the feet of veteran halfback Daly Cherry-Evans.

As the Roosters resisted the urge to rush Sam Walker back for Saturday's sudden-death semi-final with Cronulla, Tedesco revealed how Cherry-Evans had shouldered the blame for last Sunday's 19-12 defeat to the Panthers.

Cherry-Evans gave away a seven-tackle set in the final 10 minutes with Penrith halfback Nathan Cleary converting a field goal soon afterwards.

The 37-year-old Cherry-Evans then sprayed his own attempt wide when his side needed him to stay calm under pressure, which sent the Roosters into a sudden-death final against the Sharks.

"Straight away he accepted it, and as a team, you don't dump that all on him," Tedesco said.

"He's done that numerous times earlier in the year and nailed it in getting us where we needed to.

"But with Chez, with his experience and how comfortable he is in those situations, we have full confidence in whatever he decides to do.

"We know he's kicked a lot, but he's missed a few as well.

"I think with Chez's experience and his age, you can't hold on to those things. I think that's important for all of us."

Walker, meanwhile, has been left on ice for a further week after coach Trent Robinson had hinted the Queensland No. 7 was an outside chance of returning against Cronulla.

The 24-year-old Walker underwent ankle surgery after suffering a syndesmosis in a loss to the Dolphins last month.

"It's only been a couple of weeks, so he's probably got another week or so I'm guessing," Tedesco said.

"But he started to do some running, which is really quick after surgery, so we'll just see how he goes in progressing to give himself a chance."

Walker's absence means the Roosters will again be without one of their most dynamic threats when they face the Sharks with Robinson forced to rely on the relatively untested partnership of Cherry-Evans and Hugo Savala.

With the first-choice halves pairing of Walker and Cherry-Evans, the Roosters have scored at a tick over 26 points per game this season.

But with Savala and Cherry-Evans as a playmaking duo, Robinson's sides are scoring an average of just 16 points per game across three fixtures.

"He (Savala) has done his job and that's all we can ask, and that's why we love playing with him," Tedesco said.

"He'll do whatever it takes for the team, we love him as a person, as a player, and he's only going to keep getting better.

"I thought he was awesome. He'll be disappointed with some moments that he didn't nail, but overall, he's excited to get on the job this Saturday and play his part."

Back-rower Angus Crichton, who was a late scratching against Penrith, has been named in jersey No.17 by Robinson.
